subject: lotusPond
pitch:
Category: Plant.
Subject: lotus pond with a frog.
Style: Chinese ink painting.
reasoning:
I'm sketching out the plan for a lotus pond scene with a frog rendered in Chinese ink painting style, thinking through the composition: a water disc for the pond, lotus leaves, and careful use of the SDK to keep the code well-formed and error-free.

I'm deciding on the plant and frog proportions—lotus pads, stems, flowers, seed pods, and buds scaled around a 1.4 m pond disc, with a small jointed frog resting on a leaf, built skeleton-first with spine, head, jaw, and leg joints in rest pose.

Keeping the rig simple, I'll use a single root joint at the pond's origin with plant geometry attached to it directly, and the frog's joints nested underneath. The water itself becomes a low stylized cylinder from y=0 to about 0.06, with the floating leaf and frog sitting near that water line.

For the ink-style rendering, I'll paint the water as a pale wash disc with a darker rim and concentric ripple lines radiating around each leaf's position for a mottled, hand-painted look. The lotus leaves themselves work well as shallow lathed dishes with a slight center dimple, though I need to figure out how to fake a wavy, non-symmetric edge since lathe geometry is naturally circular.

Writing leaf vein shaders...

Defining the leaf profile curve...

For tilted leaves I'll approximate distance from center in 3D using the hypotenuse across x, y, z offsets divided by radius. For shading the underside, I'll check if the normal's dot product with the axis vector is sufficiently negative, painting it a pale grey-green. Now I'm defining the ink wash palette—dark ink, mid-tone, green washes from dark to pale, paper tone, water blue-grey, and petal colors ranging from pink to tip-red to a soft white base.

I'm also thinking about adding a vermilion seal, a traditional touch in ink paintings, as a small decal on the pond's front rim rather than using SVG text (to avoid font issues)—instead drawing it as a red square with simple white abstract cutout strokes to suggest a stamped character.

Now I'm shaping the pond itself as a lathed disk with a flat top, painting it in pale celadon-grey with ink-wash ripple rings radiating from the lily pads and a darker ink edge along the rim, evoking the empty-space aesthetic of ink painting with a subtle radial vignette and concentric ripple rings.

I'm also adding ripples where the lotus stems meet the water. For texel density, I'm checking painted area across the pond and foliage against the 1024/2048 atlas size to make sure the ripple lines stay crisp at roughly 1.4m scale, leaning toward 2048 for sharper detail despite the heavier cost.

Now I'm laying out the pond composition: a central floating frog leaf with the frog perched on it facing forward, plus a couple smaller floating leaves offset around it, and tall standing leaves rising on stems nearby.

I'm placing lotus blooms in a back cluster, assigning stem heights and positions so the main full bloom and a half-open companion read clearly from the viewer's angle without crowding the floating leaves.

Checking that pod placement avoids overlap with leaf C, I'm adding a low curled leaf on the left and a floating leaf with a frog near the front. The pond radius should comfortably fit all elements within roughly ±1.3 units, and I'm working out how to tilt leaves by orienting the lathe axis toward the forward direction so the bowls open naturally toward the viewer.

Now I'm planning the stems: each curves from a point at the water surface up to the underside center of its peltate leaf, built as a tapered sweep with small prickle-like spikes riding along the tube surface, roughly 8 spikes per stem across 6 stems for a manageable part count.

For the frog, I'm thinking through the skeleton setup — a root joint at the origin with child joints parented explicitly so each part knows its bone, since aim defaults could get ambiguous otherwise. Then I shift to thinking about how to build the lotus flower itself, considering whether petals should be extruded leaf-shaped outlines or lathed forms.

Each petal is a teardrop extrusion tapering in thickness, oriented with a width axis tangent to the receptacle and a length axis leaning outward and upward based on azimuth and tilt angles, with the thickness axis derived from their cross product.

Defining the petal width function...

I'll add soft vein lines along petal width at fractional positions for texture, then plan three rings of petals with varying tilt angles and sizes—outer wide-open, middle medium, inner tighter—to build a layered lotus bloom.

For each flower I'm defining a function taking center, scale, and openness, assembling the 21 petal parts plus a yellow receptacle cone, a ring of 20 thin stamen spikes, and a seed pod. A second bloom gets scaled down and less tilted for a half-open look, while the bud uses the same petal function with much smaller tilt angles, tighter scale, and green sepals plus a pink-to-green tip color transition.

For the dried seed pod I'm lathing an inverted cone shape with a flat top disc, then adding seven small dark cylinders as seed holes arranged in a center-plus-ring pattern on that flat surface. I'm keeping the pod's stem and axis straight rather than bent, and now building the stamen ring as thin yellow spikes surrounding the yellow receptacle cone frustum.

Since items from a literal frame have no bone assignment, I need to think through whether geometry will snap to the nearest joint correctly, and decide it's safer to explicitly pass the root bone into the spike options to avoid any ambiguity near the frog's joints.

For the ring tilt angle, I'm reasoning that each item's outward axis gets leaned toward the ring's line direction by the tilt amount, so a tilt near 75-80 degrees would make the stamens point mostly upward while still radiating outward from their position — which matches what I want for the spike geometry.

Now moving to the frog: I'm sketching its rest pose as a chunky stylized sitting frog about 0.16m long, positioned on the leaf's surface, with a single root joint at the pond origin and a skeleton branching into hips, spine segments, head/jaw, and separate hind and front leg chains (thigh, shin, foot, toes) since frogs lack a distinct neck.

I'm computing the frog's body placement with hips low and back, chest raised, and head lifted forward, then sweeping the spine chain through these points with varying elliptical radii to shape the body, while planning a separate upper head and lower jaw piece for the wide, flat head.

For the mouth interior, I'll add a dark reddish ellipsoid placed between the jaw and upper head at the joint, and sweep a thin ink-colored curve along the seam line from corner to corner to define the mouth edge visibly.

Computing seam curve points on the ellipsoid surface...

For the head joint, I'll define an absolute-position helper so I can place parts in model space without worrying about rotation mismatches, attaching pieces to the head bone directly. Then I'm placing bulging eyes atop the head with golden iris spheres and flattened black ellipsoid pupils for the slit effect.

For the eye texture itself, I'll decal an SVG drawing onto the eyeball surface -- a golden ellipse with a horizontal black pupil and ink outline, sized and oriented to face outward from the head. I'm also considering adding a skin-colored eyelid dome as a partial hemisphere sitting over the top half of each eye.

Actually, simpler to use a flattened ellipsoid for the brow ridge above each eye, then place small dark spheres for nostrils near the top-front of the snout, computing their position from the head ellipsoid's surface equation.

For the body, I'm layering paint effects: a mottled green base with dark ink-like blotches for the back, then applying a countershading effect to lighten the belly, mimicking an ink-wash frog illustration style.

Now I'm thinking about the paint texel density for baking spots at fine scale, and planning out the hind leg pose — folded sitting position with thigh, shin, and foot positioned in frog-local coordinates relative to the hip joint on the leaf surface.

Now I'm figuring out how the chain helper assigns names to joints along a leg path — working out how many names correspond to the spans between hip, knee, ankle, and toe so the naming convention stays consistent across all limb chains.

I'm settling on a hip-knee-ankle-toe path with four named joints, using a polyline so knots sit exactly at each joint. For skinning, I'm defining a radius profile that tapers smoothly from thigh to shin to foot using an evenly-keyed array of thickness values.

For the foot, I'm fanning out four toe rods from the ankle base with a spread angle, each capped with a small rounded pad, and adding thin flat webbing polygons stretched between adjacent toe tips for a membrane-like detail.

I'll skip toe joints for now and keep them rigid on the foot joint. For front legs, I'm sketching pillar-like chains from shoulder to elbow to wrist to fanning fingers with lighter rounded pad tips, then starting on the body spine chain with a rump point as the first anchor.

Now I'm defining the rest of the spine chain through hips, mid-body, chest, and head, then working out a radius function to control the body's width and height taper along that sweep.

I'll orient the body's cross-section so the horizontal radius follows the binormal and vertical follows the normal, keeping the caps rounded. For texture, I'm skipping a throat sac but scattering a handful of small wart bumps across the back using a surface filter that only places them where the normal points upward, plus adding darker ink-spot details in a muted green tone.

Thinking about the overall ink-painting aesthetic, I want to add calligraphic elements like tapered brush strokes for stems, leaf veins, water ripples, and a vermilion seal stamp to sell the style. I'm now planning out the texture budget—aiming for 5-12 total—including the frog's eye, the seal, and ripple cards made from broken-stroke ellipses to suggest water motion near the stem bases.

Settling on a final texture lineup: eye, seal, and the broken-ring ripples, while deciding mist and duckweed details aren't worth the added complexity given the alpha cutoff limitations.

I should keep the code manageable in length and prioritize correctness. I'm setting up the imports from the SDK and double-checking which helper functions like mix, noise, smoothstep, and paint are actually exported from the index.

Now I'm defining the color palette as constants, then writing the paint logic for the water ripples, blending colors based on surface normal and distance from ripple centers.

I'm adding a thin dark ink ring at the pond's rim edge, and shaping the pond as a lathe-generated bowl with a flat bottom and simple edge profile, keeping segment counts reasonable so ripple painting still reads well.

For floating leaves, I'm positioning them just above the water surface with a slight raised rim near the edge, leaving the leaf center flat so the frog can sit directly on top at the leaf's height.

Writing leaf profile code...

Writing leaf shading logic...

I should also darken the rim near the leaf edge with an ink-toned blend, and add a dark central nub where distance is very small. For the stems, I'll give them a gradient from dark ink near the water up to a lighter green tone toward the top, rather than a flat fill.

Writing stem sweep function...

Still writing spike placement logic...

Writing lathe parameters...

Now I'm designing the lotus bloom function with concentric petal rings, each specified by count, length, width, and tilt angle, scaled by an overall size factor and blended by how open the flower is.

For each petal, I'm computing its orientation vectors from the azimuth and tilt angle, then placing it around the flower center with a thickness taper and slight bevel for a soft, rounded petal shape.

For cupping, I could split each petal into two segments—a lower half and an upper half with different tilt angles—so the tip curls inward or outward relative to the base, giving a cupped shape. That doubles the part count per bloom but stays manageable across two blooms, so I'll define the lower segment covering roughly 55% of the petal length at one tilt and the upper segment continuing with a curled tilt, slicing the outline accordingly.

Writing the outline-generation function...

Still writing outline logic...

I'll overlap the segments slightly so the tilt transition hides the gap, then write the paint function that computes the local width fraction along the petal to shade edges differently near the tip. Writing petal paint logic...

Edge pixels near the outline get a deeper pink ink tint for definition, while the base-to-tip gradient shifts from a cream base through soft pink to a deeper rose, with subtle vein darkening at specific fractional positions. Now I'm turning to the receptacle, which I'll build as a small lathed cone frustum.

I'm adding a yellow-green seed pod at the center with a simple outline shape and dotted texture on top, then a ring of eighteen gold stamen spikes tilted mostly upright around the receptacle. I'm keeping the bloom itself upright, positioning its center just above the stem's top point where the receptacle sits.

Now I'm working out the bud shapes — closed petal rings in groups of 5, 5, 4 with steep tilts near vertical, scaling tilt and openness together so a fully closed bud sits at about 6 degrees of lean with petals overlapping at the base to stay sealed shut.

I'm defining how petals curl per ring: outer petals flare slightly outward while inner rings curl inward to cup the bud tip closed, with buds getting an even stronger inward curl plus a pale green-tinged color variant at their base.

Now I'm building the pod geometry: a tapered lathe shape rising from the stem to a rimmed top, painted with a mottled yellow-green to grey ink, topped with a small cluster of dark seed cylinders arranged in a center-plus-ring pattern.

I'm also laying out floating lily pads around the pond—one near the frog at (0.12, 0.45) radius 0.4, plus several others with varying sizes and tilts—checking that each stays within the 1.35 pond radius boundary.

Then I'm verifying the pads don't overlap: nudging the leaf near (-0.15, 0.95) to (-0.2, 1.0) so it clears the frog's leaf, and confirming the other nearby leaves keep enough distance apart.

Now I'm placing some ripple cards flat near the stem bases and the frog's leaf to add texture, working out how the card's size and orientation should align along the flow direction versus perpendicular to it.

Writing ripple SVG code...

For the seal, I'm sketching a red rounded square with a lighter paper-toned abstract character cut into it using simple strokes, keeping it as a flat textured plane.

Now I'm placing it as a small "stone chop" tablet near the pond rim's edge, positioning its corner to just touch the water boundary while sitting at a slight height off the ground.

I'm checking the seal's position against the pond radius to make sure it doesn't overlap — moving it to (1.0, y, 1.1) keeps it clear at distance ~1.41 versus the 1.35 pond edge, and I'm adding a slight 20° rotation for a more natural placement.

Now I'm thinking about decorative ink dots for the floating leaves, placing small ellipse clusters near the leaf rims where they're relatively flat so the cards sit correctly, computing their y-height based on the leaf's dish curvature at roughly 80% of the radius.

For the frog, I'm considering adding a pale lower jaw for the throat and two thin dorsal fold lines sweeping along the back sides for extra anatomical detail, while deciding to skip extras like lotus petal textures or fallen petals on the water.

Using the spine chain as bone should work fine even with the path crossing joints. For the eyes, I'll place decals using the head bone, positioning them near the eye center offset outward by the surface normal, with a default up vector and moderate segment count for the gold iris and black pupil texture.

Now I'm thinking through the eyeball geometry as a small sphere with a gold base color under the decal, and planning the spine joint hierarchy -- a root joint at origin with a chain parented to it starting at the rump position.

Adding the head joint attached to the chest end, extending forward to form the head ellipsoid, but the total frog length from rump to head tip comes out to about 0.33m, which feels too long -- I need to scale things down a bit.

Setting the frog's overall length to about 0.25m works better against the 0.8-0.9m lotus leaves. Defining more body chain points...

Still working out head geometry: placing the head joint and computing the upper skull ellipsoid center and radii, then positioning the lower jaw ellipsoid and its hinge point relative to the head joint so the jaw aims forward correctly.

I'm computing the mouth line where the upper and lower jaw ellipsoids meet, using trigonometry to trace the intersection curve along the skull's surface at a fixed vertical offset, generating sample points around the arc for the visible mouth seam.

So the jaw pokes out below where the mouth line sits, which works fine visually. I'm placing bulging eyes near the top of the head, angled outward, with brow ellipsoids above them, and checking that the frog's body sits just above the leaf surface.

Now I'm mapping out the hind leg joint chain—hip, knee, ankle, and toe positions—to get a natural seated frog pose with limbs splayed outward.

Defining the sweep radii as functions of chain length...

I'll finish the leg radius taper with a few more keyframes toward the shin and knee, then reuse the frog skin pattern with countershading for the legs so the spotting continues naturally, with paler undersides. For the hind feet, I'm placing four toes per foot with varying lengths and outward spread angles, innermost toes angled toward the body.

Writing toe pads and webbing...

I'll grab the last joint in the hind chain instead of using the tip accessor directly, since that avoids the null type issue. Now I'm placing the front leg joints — shoulder angled back-out and forearm straight down-forward so the frog looks propped up naturally.

Defining arm chain geometry...

Now I'm positioning the frog on the leaf, setting its base coordinates and a helper for offsetting points relative to that origin, while thinking through how the leaf's dish shape and the frog's toe placement relate to this base.

I'm defining the pale belly countershading and darker mottled back spots, then working on scattering warts across the frog's surface using a sweep-based body shape.

Now I'm tallying up the total mesh count across the scene: pond, ripples, lily pads, stems with prickles, and both the fully open and half-open flower blooms with their petals, receptacles, seeds, and stamens.

Sticking to roughly 300 parts keeps me well under a 1000-piece budget, and checking triangle counts from the lathe-based leaves and extruded petals confirms the geometry stays light. I'm also verifying the flat color palette stays under the 64-color cap — since paint-based materials don't count against that limit, I'm well within bounds with under 20 distinct flat colors like ink, gold, seed tones, and wart coloring.

I'm noting that each petal generates its own unique paint object for length, width, and offset values, which means many near-duplicate paints get baked separately into the paint sheet — slightly wasteful, but not a blocker.

I realize I can cache paints by key since they're really just function calls, and all painted parts get baked into one shared texture regardless. Running the numbers on total painted surface area across petals, leaves, pond, and frog gives roughly 14 m², which works out to a texel density around 2.2mm with a 2048 paint size — comfortably fine. I also want to make sure the ink-wash aesthetic comes through, especially calligraphic tapered strokes on the stems, and I'm now working out the tilt parameters for each standing leaf — position, height, radius, tilt axis, and dish shape.

Defining stem curve control points for each leaf...

I'm placing a young rolled lotus shoot near (0.3,-0.1), built as a thin stem topped with a small pale-green spike to suggest an unfurling leaf, then positioning the main lotus bloom stem starting around (0.05,-0.55) rising up to its flower head near y=1.16-1.18.

Now I'm checking that this bloom isn't hidden behind Leaf B, which tilts across negative x at that height, and confirming the bloom's petal radius keeps it clear of overlap. I'm then working out placement for a second, half-open bloom, testing a spot near x=-0.15 that risks colliding with Leaf B, and considering instead tucking it near Leaf C's span around x=0.55 where there's more open space.

Since the tilt leans the leaf's normal toward +z, that edge sits lower, so I'm testing (0.5, 0.55, 0.3) for the second bloom position, checking it doesn't collide with the frog near (0.12, .45).

Checking the distance from the bloom stem base to the leaf center confirms it clears outside the leaf radius, so the bloom should visually hover above and to the right of the frog without obscuring it given the petal radius and offset.

Checking the pod distance from the main bloom clears the petal radius, and the pond radius also fits fine. Now placing a rolled shoot element and verifying its coordinates don't overlap nearby shapes.

I'm settling on the title "Lotus Pond with Frog" and skipping an inscription seal for now. Starting to write the TypeScript scene code...

Setting up ink wash colors and the builder config...

Still defining pond geometry...

I'm thinking about adding a dark ink-brush border ring at the pond's edge beyond a certain radius, then planning ripple card positions near the stem bases, and starting a leaf paint function that shades leaves based on normal direction and distance from center with noise-based color mixing.

Still writing leaf shader logic...

Writing outline builder...

Building the receptacle and stamen ring now...
